I think this is a decent game that I would recommend to people who are a fan of classic NES platformers, but probably wouldn't recommend that outside of that sphere. The game doesn't do anything particularly outstanding, but isn't particularly offensive for the most part either; plays decent, looks okay, decent soundtrack. One huge thing to note is that this game is pretty short, only being 5 levels; but on the flipside of that, if you lose all of your lives, it's back to square one. I personally am not a fan of not having unlimited continues, but with a game this short and likely going for the classic NES style in the most literal interpretation, I can kinda see where they were coming from with that decision. Another thing is that your starting character just flat out sucks. He has a weird arcing projectile that's akin to the rock from Friday the 13th NES and about just as useful. However, as you go through the game, you start to get more characters as you go on, especially if you find the secret areas, and the character get progressively better (the Skeleton you can get in Level 2 I would argue is the first truly viable character). I ended up beating the game with one of the characters added in the free DLC update, the Protagonist, who is actually quite good and even ended up getting the secret ending first time by finding all 6 secret runes. Once you start getting some actually good characters, the game is actually decently fun, though, as stated before, incredibly short. I also am not a fan that you can only unlock one character per run of the game, though at least if you find a character unlock area after unlocking a character in that run, you get an extra life, which is nice. But because you can only unlock one character per run, if you're like me and managed to beat the game after unlocking only a few characters, then, unless you really want to achievement hunt this game, there's no point in going back to unlock everyone else once you've beaten the game. This game does have a decent amount of achievements to hunt if you're into that sort of thing and can extend the life of this game for a bit, but as a whole, the time you get out of this game is likely going to be quite short. If you're a retro platformer junkie, you'll likely get some enjoyment out of this game once you get a viable character, but you probably won't get much out of this game otherwise.

Short version: Do NOT get this game. You can't save your progress, the levels are frustrating death traps, and it really seems like the developers tried to ensure you won't enjoy yourself at all while playing it. Stay away from this P.O.S. 

Long version: Despite being a modern game, all the frustrating features shown in 'classic' games are still here and thriving. Bad level designs, dickishly placed enemies, frustrating gimmicks, useless attacks, knock back from enemy attacks sending you flying into a pit of spikes, and much more are all here to make sure that you will not enjoy yourself in the slightest.

There is also a HUGE issue that the games doesn't save your progress, so if you made the same mistake as I did, and got about halfway thru the game and tried to come back to it later, you'll find all your progress has been flushed down the toilet and you have to start all over again. It's not a long game, but there is NO excuse for this and makes the game an absolute chore since it apparently expects you to finish the whole thing in one sitting. 

I LOVE Halloween and retro games, and have tried several times to enjoy this, but it gives me a headache ever damn time due to all the frustrating features and hair pulling concepts that the developers though was a good idea to include.

Do yourself a favor and DO NOT get the game. DO NOT be suckered in by the cute art style and/or gooey reviews talking about 8-bit nostalgia. There are MUCH better games out there, that need more attention than this frustrating, half bake mess.

[i][h1]A classic and original game but you’ll love it for a little while.[/h1][/i]

From its art-style to well made music, it just screams from the classic 8-bit gaming era. I truly admire the originality of the game. As a traditional 8-bit game, you have your simple controls: move, jump and shoot. Simple and fun... but I only have two dislikes about this game.

This may vary from player to player, its difficulty. I find it easy once you’ve memorized the layout of the stages and where the creatures spawn. Especially when fighting the bosses. Their movements and attack patterns becomes too predictable to avoid. It does offer a mode called “hardcore mode”. In hardcore mode it sets the health points to one but the number of lives remain default. If you get hit or touch anything that’s lethal, you die. It’s simple and straightforward. I only died once, and again, it’s easy when you memorize the game well enough.

Aside from its difficulty, my biggest disappointment with the game that it’s short. It only has five stages and each stage has two bosses. You’ll probably get about one or two hours of enjoyment. That's excluding the number of playthroughs for each character. It’s really disappointing to see a well thought out game to be so short. I only wish the game was much longer.

I believe the length of the game and difficulty is what holding it back from being a great, little game. Its art and music, nevertheless, hold true to the 8-bit classic gaming era. If you're planning on getting it, just prepare not to fall in love with the game.

Halloween Forever isn't going to blow your mind.

But does it have to? Is there a rule out there that says every game HAS to be a paradigm shift?

Actually, that feels unfair to Halloween Forever, because as far as games go, this character, this type of shooter, in this setting, IS actually pretty unique. It may lack the ambition of a retro-esque game like Shovel Knight, but it's still enjoyable. Halloween Forever is a short, simple, and charming little game about Halloween with 8-bit graphics and chiptune music. That's all it wants to be and it does its job well.

It may be easy for some people to write this off as "just another cheap pixel art game," but it's obvious to see the love and attention it was given by the developer. Simple as it may be, this is a tough little game to finish, particularly because it doesn't save your progress -- a move that was done intentionally. It'll remember which secret characters you've unlocked, but as far as actually playing this game goes, it gives you no quarter. 1ups are scarce, death comes quickly, and there are no continues. Game Over means starting back at level 1.

Shockingly, the game doesn't feel cheap for doing this. Halloween Forever isn't a game that feels mean, or like it's punishing you for being less than perfect. It just asks that you value every move you take, and play smart. If you could blow through the whole game on your first try, it'd probably take less than an hour, so a little bit of failure and overcoming the challenge is part of the fun. Observe, learn, and do better next time. There's no masochism here, just focus. 

There's plenty to do, too. Alternate routes and secret areas are plentiful (vital for getting things like the game's true ending), and a handful thoughtful achievements will push you to play the game in new, weird ways. 

For five bucks? Less, if it's on sale? You won't see many articles celebrating this as a masterclass in anything, but it's well worth the price.
